t: Every night for 14 months, you've said goodnight to a star.
It sits low over the horizon, small and blue-white,
brighter than anything else in the Martian sky.
Your mom told you what it was on your very first night on Mars.
That's Earth, sweetheart. That's home.
Tonight, you step into the observation room,
press your forehead against the glass,
and look for it. It isn't there.
You check the other side of the sky.
You check the telescope on the roof.
You check the spot where it should be over and over until your eyes burn.
Just stars. Cold, far away, completely ordinary stars.
Earth is gone. And here's what you don't know yet.
In the next two years, you'll nearly die in the biggest dust storm in Martian history.
You'll hear 40 people say the names of everyone they loved,
one by one, for eight hours straight.
And on the last night of the first Martian year,
you'll look up and see something rising in the sky that was never supposed to be there.
But first, you have to survive Sol 1.
That's what Mars calls a day.
It lasts 24 hours and 39 minutes a little longer than ours.
Your station has 40 people.
Scientists, engineers, a doctor, a cook, and four kids, including you.
You've been here for 14 months.
You came because your mom studies plants and your dad fixes machines.
And nobody else wanted to move a teenager to another planet.
You agreed because you were 15.
And it sounded like the greatest adventure ever.
In the morning, Commander Hale gathers everyone in the dining room.
Her voice is calm, but her hands are shaking.
Mission control hasn't answered in 19 hours.
Here's something about Mars that you learn quickly.
A message from Earth takes anywhere from three to 22 minutes to arrive,
depending on where the planets are.
So a conversation with home is never a conversation.
It's more like a letter than a call.
Hale explains they waited an hour.
Then six.
Then 19.
The radio dish antennas are working.
Every signal is going out.
Signal goes out.
Nothing comes back.
The telescope operator, a quiet woman named Anna, stands up.
I looked where Earth should be.
It's not faint.
It's not hiding behind a cloud.
There's nothing there.
What about the moon?
Someone asks.
Gone too.
Nobody speaks.
Then your mom who's sitting next to you takes your hand.
Her palm is cold and wet.
She says very quietly, okay, okay, okay.
Nobody ever finds out why.
By Sol III, the shock turns into math.
Commander Hale draws a list on the whiteboard.
Food enough for 14 months.
Water pulled from underground ice,
which the station mines every day.
Oxygen made on site from the Martian air,
which is 95% carbon dioxide.
A small experiment on one of the real rovers
has already shown it works.
Turning the thin Martian air into breathable oxygen,
a few grams at a time.
Your station has a much bigger version,
but it needs power and power needs the sun,
which on Mars is only half as bright as at home.
At the bottom, she writes one more line.
Resupply ship, 18 months.
She doesn't say what everyone is thinking.
The ship was built on Earth.
Out there, past the airlock, the planet doesn't care.
The air is thinner than at the top
of the tallest mountains on Earth,
less than 1% of the pressure you were born with.
If you stepped outside without a suit,
you'd lose consciousness in about 15 seconds.
The average temperature is about 60 degrees below zero.
There's no magnetic field to protect you from the sun.
So every day on the surface,
you absorb as much radiation as several chest X-rays,
and the red dust that looks like cinnamon
is full of chemicals called perchlorates,
which are poisonous to people.
It's the most beautiful place you've ever seen.
A canyon almost as long as the United States is wide,
volcanoes taller than any mountain on Earth,
and everything in it is trying to kill you.
On Sol 9, two engineers decide to go home.
They don't say it that way.
They say they wanna check the launch pad,
but everyone knows they take a rover
across the plain, through the dust, to the old landing site
where the ship that brought them here
still sits half-buried in sand.
You watch them on the radio.
One of them laughs.
It's fine, it's fine, huh?
We'll just fly back.
Then the other one is quiet for a long time.
There's nothing to fly back to, he says.
They drive back to the station without talking.
That night, everyone eats dinner together
for the first time in a week.
Nobody leaves the table until the plates are empty.
That night, you can't sleep.
You climb to the roof dome and watch the sky,
and for the first time you notice
something you've been too distracted to see.
A small, lumpy moon shaped like a potato,
racing across the sky.
It's Phobos, one of Mars's two tiny moons.
It circles the planet so fast that it rises in the West
and sets in the East three times a day.
Your dad used to point it out when you first arrived.
The moon that rises in the West, he'd say.
Everything here is a little upside down.
Tonight, he comes up and sits beside you
without saying a word.
He holds a thermos of hot chocolate.
You share it and you watch Phobos disappear.
I keep thinking someone's going to call, he says.
I keep checking my phone.
Me too.
The days become sols, and the sols become weeks,
and you learn to live on a planet with no home.
Mars' gravity is only 38% of Earth's.
At first, you bounce everywhere.
Your mom says it's like being underwater,
but you can breathe.
Low gravity makes bones thinner and muscles weaker.
So every morning, all 40 people spend two hours
on treadmills and weight machines.
The cook yells at them to eat more protein.
Your dad, who used to hate exercise,
becomes the most dedicated man in the building.
One afternoon, your dad welds a basketball hoop
out of scrap metal and hangs it in the biggest tunnel.
In 38% gravity, you can jump almost three times as high.
The four kids on the base play until they're dizzy.
Even Commander Hale joins in once
in her work boots and dunks.
Everyone cheers.
Later that night, you find her alone in the hallway,
leaning against the wall with her face in her hands.
She sees you and wipes her eyes.
Don't tell anyone, she says.
Somebody has to look like they're sure.
You nod, you never tell anyone.
And your mom plants potatoes, it's an old idea.
Scientists have grown them in soil
made to imitate Martian dirt.
First, you wash out the perchlorates.
Then you mix and compost,
which is every scrap of food
and everything else that used to be alive.
By Sol 40, there are green leaves in the greenhouse.
By Sol 60, your mom is crying
because she's growing something
that wasn't there yesterday.
This is the first plant, she says,
that will ever grow on this planet
for people who have never seen Earth.
Then on Sol 70, the sky turns brown.
It starts as a small smudge on the horizon.
Within a day, it's a wall.
Within three, the whole sky is dark.
Mars has the biggest dust storms in the solar system.
Every few years, they can swallow the whole planet.
They last for weeks, even months.
The dust blocks the sun and the solar panels starve.
Power drops to a quarter.
Heating drops with it.
Commander Hale makes a hard decision.
They turn off everything that isn't life support.
Lights, labs, even the greenhouse heaters.
People sleep in the same room to stay warm.
40 people wrapped in blankets
on the floor of the dining hall.
The wind screams outside
like something big trying to get in.
On the 31st night of the storm, the greenhouse freezes.
Your mom runs in.
You follow her.
The leaves are black.
The soil is hard as stone.
A month of work, ruined.
She falls to her knees and pulls out the first potato plant
and her hands are shaking so badly
it breaks apart in her fingers.
You kneel next to her.
You don't know what to say.
For the first time, you notice how thin she's become.
How tired.
How she hasn't talked about earth in weeks.
I miss Grandma, you whisper.
She puts her arm around you.
I know.
I never said goodbye.
I know.
And you both cry in the dark, in the cold,
on a planet that wasn't made for you.
Then from the back of the greenhouse,
you hear a very small sound, a crack.
You turn on your flashlight.
In the corner under a table, behind an old crate,
one potato plant is still green.
One out of 300, your mom stares at it.
Then she starts to laugh and she can't stop.
The storm ends on Sol 109.
When the sky clears, it's the first sunrise
anyone has seen in a month.
The light is soft and orange.
For a long time, no one speaks.
Then Anna, the telescope operator, goes up on the roof
and doesn't come down for three hours.
That night, Commander Hale calls everyone to the dining hall.
We've been surviving, she says.
I don't want us to only survive.
I want us to remember.
So they hold a ceremony.
It has no name at first.
Later, people will call it the night of names.
One by one, every person stands up
and says the names of the people they left on earth.
Parents, husbands, wives, children, best friends,
a dog, a teacher who changed someone's life.
Some people can only say one.
Some say 50.
A man named Dr. Singh, who's always been serious,
stands calling out names, his old village in India.
Every single person, he remembers them all.
It lasts eight hours.
When it's your turn, you stand up and your voice cracks.
Grandma Lila, Aunt May, my best friend Daniel,
my teacher, Mr. Carver, who said I'd go to space someday.
And Pepper, the dog next door,
who never liked anyone but me.
Everyone laughs a little.
Everyone cries a little.
When the last name is said, nobody moves.
Hale lights a small lamp on the table.
As long as one of us is alive, she says,
none of them are gone.
It's the first time in months
that you feel something other than fear.
After that, the station changes.
People stop whispering.
People start planning.
They dig new tunnels underground
where the rock blocks radiation.
They build bigger greenhouses.
They figure out how to melt ice faster,
how to grow beans, wheat, lettuce, even strawberries.
The cook invents a recipe for potato bread
that people line up for.
Dad builds a new generator out of old rover parts.
Anna charts the sky every night,
looking for any sign of home.
And slowly, the 40 of you
becomes something more than a crew.
You become a town.
On Sol 500 Anna, the telescope operator has a baby.
It's the first human born on Mars.
A little girl, six pounds with a full head of dark hair.
Everyone crowds around the glass
of the medical room, whispering.
Anna's husband holds the baby up
so the whole room can see her.
What's her name?
Commander Hale asks.
Anna smiles.
Tara, the word for Earth.
And for the first time,
the whole room is crying and laughing at the same time.
A Martian year lasts 687 days,
almost twice as long as ours.
On the last evening of the first one,
the whole station climbs to the surface in suits
and stands on a hill above the base.
You're holding Tara in a special baby suit,
even though she's too young to understand.
The sky is clear, the sun is going down.
And here's something strange about Mars.
The sunset is blue.
The dust in the air scatters light
so that the sky around the sun turns a deep, glowing blue
while the rest of the world fades to red.
It's the opposite of Earth.
Your mom stands next to you.
That's what home looked like, she says.
Like this, the sky, just the other way around.
Tara looks up.
She has never seen Earth.
She never will.
But she looks at the blue sky with huge, curious eyes
and you realize something.
This is her home and it always will be.
Do you think we'll ever know what happened, you ask?
Your mom shrugs.
Maybe, maybe not.
But we're still here.
Then the radio on your suit crackles.
It's Anna's voice from the observatory.
She sounds strange, out of breath. Everyone, look east, right now.
Look east, right now.
You turn around.
At the edge of the sky where the stars are coming out,
there's a point of light that wasn't there yesterday.
It's not blue-white.
It's not Earth.
It's orange and it's steady and it's getting brighter.
It's moving, Anna says.
Straight toward us.
Nobody speaks.
Your hand tightens around Tara's tiny glove.
So what would you do if you woke up on Mars
and Earth was gone?
Tell us in the comments.
And if you'd have said the names too,
hit like and subscribe for part two.
